topic: Why deep ocean water is dark blue
research_summary: The ocean's deep blue color is not a reflection of the sky — it is an intrinsic optical property of water itself. Water molecules absorb red, orange, and yellow wavelengths of light progressively as depth increases, because longer-wavelength photons carry just the right energy to excite water's O-H bond vibrations. Blue light (~450nm) has the lowest absorption coefficient of any visible wavelength in pure water (~0.013 m⁻¹ vs ~0.65 m⁻¹ for red at 700nm), meaning it travels roughly 50x further before being absorbed. The result is a light-peeling cascade: dive to 5m and red is gone, 25m and orange vanishes, 50m and yellow disappears — leaving only a deepening blue. This layered stripping of color is the video's core visual opportunity: a visceral, countdown-style descent that audiences can feel.

data_points.claim: The absorption coefficient of pure water at 700nm (red) is approximately 0.65 m⁻¹, versus only 0.013 m⁻¹ at 450nm (blue) — meaning red light is absorbed about 50x more rapidly than blue light over the same water column.
data_points.source_name: Pope & Fry 1997, Applied Optics — absorption spectrum of pure water
data_points.usable_as: stat_card — the 50x ratio is the anchor fact that makes the mechanism vivid

data_points.claim: Red wavelengths are effectively gone by 5-10 meters depth in clear ocean water. Orange disappears by ~25m, yellow by ~50m, green by ~75-100m. Only blue light penetrates to the base of the photic zone (~200m).
data_points.source_name: NOAA Ocean Service — How far does light travel in the ocean?
data_points.usable_as: hook — the layered stripping of color is the video's core visual metaphor

data_points.claim: The photic zone, where enough sunlight penetrates for photosynthesis, extends only to about 200 meters — less than 5% of average ocean depth (3,688m). Below 1,000m, zero sunlight reaches.
data_points.usable_as: closing_punch — the scale of dark ocean vs lit ocean is humbling

data_points.claim: Water molecules absorb red-light photons because those photons carry energy that matches the vibrational frequency of the O-H bond in H2O — this is quantum-mechanical resonance absorption, not classical scattering.
data_points.source_name: Mobley 2006 — Light and Water: Radiative Transfer in Natural Waters
data_points.usable_as: script_anchor — the molecular explanation separates this video from 'sky reflection' oversimplifications

data_points.claim: At 10 meters depth, an underwater photograph of a red fish taken without artificial lighting shows the fish as grey-green. This is routinely demonstrated in scuba photography — red filters are used below ~10m to restore color.
data_points.source_name: B&H Photo — Underwater Photography Light Guide
data_points.usable_as: hook — the 'red fish goes grey' fact is instantly relatable and surprising

misconceptions.myth: The ocean is blue because it reflects the blue sky
misconceptions.reality: Sky reflection contributes only at the surface. Deep water would appear blue even under a completely overcast or grey sky — the color is intrinsic to water's molecular absorption properties, not borrowed from the sky.

misconceptions.myth: Deep ocean water is just dark, not specifically blue
misconceptions.reality: Throughout the photic zone (~0-200m), the water column is specifically blue — not grey, not black. The blue color persists because blue is the last wavelength to be absorbed. It only becomes truly dark below ~1,000m.

misconceptions.myth: Water absorbs light the same way at all wavelengths
misconceptions.reality: Water has a strong wavelength-dependent absorption spectrum. It is nearly transparent to blue-green light and heavily absorbs red-infrared. This selectivity is why ocean color is specifically blue, not simply 'dark'.

audience_insights.knowledge_level: General adults likely know 'it reflects the sky' (partially wrong) and know that it gets dark deep down, but don't know the wavelength-specific absorption mechanism, the precise depths at which colors vanish, or that the blue color is intrinsic to water molecules themselves.
